This section examines Experiment F —
Uniform operator portfolio from

first principles. Keep two questions
separate: does changing the order

change the measured outcome, and does the
proposed search method

beat a matched alternative at the same
distinct-evaluation budget? Question:

can one safe default avoid catastrophic
operator mismatch? Setup: portfolio

and adaptive variants across all three
typed landscapes, n=6 through

16, 15 seeds, same cap as the operator
study. Result:

the uniform portfolio had zero censoring
on every typed landscape

and cost about 1.1–4.1 times the matched
fixed operator. Adaptive

result: it ranked the correct operator
first on all three

landscapes but did not consistently
improve hitting time and required

an extra evaluation per mutation event.
Decision: use uniform portfolio

when the landscape is unknown; use a
matched fixed operator

when diagnosed; treat adaptive weights as
a diagnostic. Now read

evidence panel F-portfolio. The axes,
units, and sample are stated

on screen. The sample represented here is
15 seeds. Raw

observations remain visible wherever the
artifact provides them. Censored

observations stay marked at the cap rather
than becoming invented

hitting times, and sampled landscapes
leave unobserved permutations blank.

The supported finding is: Result: the
uniform portfolio had zero

censoring on every typed landscape and
cost about 1.1–4.1 times

the matched fixed operator. The broader
claim not established here

is: The conclusion is scoped to the
recorded evaluator, landscape,

and budget. This evidence changed the
program as follows: Decision:

use uniform portfolio when the landscape
is unknown; use a

matched fixed operator when diagnosed;
treat adaptive weights as a

diagnostic. The distinction is part of the
result. A large

ordering effect does not automatically
imply an evolutionary-search

advantage, and almost-sure convergence
does not promise practical
efficiency.
